drills.los_text: explain absolute and relative risk budgets and their use in determining and implementing an asset allocation

questions.stem: The marginal contribution to total risk (MCTR) of asset class i in a portfolio is most likely computed as:

options.A: the asset's variance divided by portfolio volatility.
options.B: the asset's beta with the portfolio times portfolio volatility.
options.C: the asset's weight times portfolio volatility.

rationales.A: Dividing an asset's own variance by portfolio volatility ignores how that asset co-moves with everything else held, which is what determines the risk it adds at the margin. An asset can be volatile on its own and still contribute little to total risk if its correlation with the rest of the portfolio is low, so this is not the MCTR.
rationales.B: MCTR for asset class i is the beta of asset class i with respect to the portfolio multiplied by portfolio return volatility. Beta is what makes the measure work: it takes account not only of the asset's own volatility but also of the asset's correlations with the other assets in the portfolio. An asset with high standalone volatility but low correlation therefore carries a lower marginal contribution than its own volatility alone would suggest.
rationales.C: Weight times portfolio volatility treats every asset class as though its beta with the portfolio were one, so it ignores both the asset's own volatility and its correlations with the rest of the holdings. Weight does enter the risk decomposition, but one step later: the absolute contribution to total risk is the weight multiplied by the MCTR.

questions.stem: The absolute contribution to total risk (ACTR) for asset class i is most likely computed as:

options.A: its marginal contribution to total risk divided by its weight.
options.B: its weight times its marginal contribution to total risk.
options.C: its squared beta times portfolio variance.

rationales.A: This inverts the relationship. Dividing the marginal contribution by the weight would make a tiny position look like a large risk contributor and a dominant position look like a small one; a contribution has to scale up with the size of the position, not down.
rationales.B: ACTR for asset class i is the weight of asset class i multiplied by its marginal contribution to total risk. The ACTR measures how much asset i contributes to portfolio return volatility, and dividing each ACTR by total portfolio risk gives the percentage of total risk that each position contributes. The decomposition is exact: the ACTRs sum to the portfolio's expected standard deviation.
rationales.C: Squared beta times portfolio variance is a variance-scaled quantity, not a contribution to portfolio standard deviation, and it also drops the position's weight entirely. Such terms do not sum across asset classes to the portfolio's expected standard deviation the way ACTRs do.

questions.stem: From a risk-budgeting perspective, an asset allocation is most likely optimal when:

options.A: each asset class is held at its market-cap weight.
options.B: each asset class contributes an equal absolute amount to total risk.
options.C: each asset class has the same ratio of excess return to MCTR.

rationales.A: Holding each asset class at its market-capitalization weight is simply market-cap weighting. It is a construction rule that says nothing about how marginal contributions to risk compare across asset classes, so it is not the risk-budgeting optimality condition.
rationales.B: Equalizing each asset class's absolute contribution to total risk (ACTR) is the risk-parity heuristic. Risk parity equalizes ACTR without any reference to expected excess returns, so an allocation can satisfy it and still fail the risk-budgeting optimality condition, which is stated in terms of return earned per unit of marginal risk taken.
rationales.C: An asset allocation is optimal from a risk-budgeting perspective when the ratio of excess return (over the risk-free rate) to the marginal contribution to total risk (MCTR) is the same for all assets, and when that common ratio equals the Sharpe ratio of the tangency portfolio. In a worked UK allocation, every asset exhibits the same 0.368 ratio at the Sharpe-ratio-maximizing allocation, which is what identifies that allocation as the optimal one.

questions.stem: A portfolio holds two asset classes, A and B, with A carrying twice the weight of B. Asset B's absolute contribution to total risk (ACTR) most likely exceeds A's when:

options.A: B's expected return is more than twice A's.
options.B: B's beta relative to the portfolio is more than twice A's.
options.C: B's correlation with the risk-free rate exceeds A's.

rationales.A: Expected return does not enter the ACTR calculation. ACTR depends on the position weight, the asset's beta with respect to the portfolio, and portfolio return volatility, so how B's expected return compares with A's is irrelevant to which position contributes more risk.
rationales.B: ACTR_i = (Weight_i)(Beta_i with respect to the portfolio)(Portfolio return volatility). Portfolio return volatility is common to both positions, so the comparison reduces to weight times beta. Because A carries twice B's weight, B's ACTR exceeds A's only if B's beta with respect to the portfolio is more than twice as large as A's beta.
rationales.C: Correlation with the risk-free rate does not enter the ACTR formula; the risk-free asset carries no volatility to correlate with. The relevant sensitivity is the asset's beta with respect to the portfolio, which embeds the asset's correlation with the portfolio, not with the risk-free rate.

questions.stem: Risk budgets may address total risk, active risk, or residual risk. The marginal contribution to a given type of risk is most likely defined as:

options.A: the historical realized volatility divided by the number of assets.
options.B: the partial derivative of the risk with respect to the holding.
options.C: the correlation coefficient between the asset and the total portfolio.

rationales.A: Dividing historical realized volatility by the number of assets is not a marginal measure at all. It is an arbitrary equal split of a backward-looking total, and it says nothing about how portfolio risk responds to a change in any one holding.
rationales.B: The marginal contribution to a given type of risk is the partial derivative of the risk in question — total risk, active risk, or residual risk — with respect to the applicable type of portfolio holding: asset allocation holdings, active holdings, or residual holdings. Knowing the marginal contribution to total risk (MCTR) allows one to (1) approximate the change in portfolio risk arising from a small change in an individual holding, (2) determine which positions are optimal, and (3) construct a risk budget.
rationales.C: The correlation between an asset and the portfolio appears inside the beta term that MCTR uses, but a correlation coefficient is not itself a marginal contribution. It is unitless and carries no information about position size or portfolio volatility, so it cannot measure how total risk changes as a holding changes.

drills.los_text: describe how client needs and preferences regarding investment risks can be incorporated into asset allocation

questions.stem: An investor's risk aversion coefficient (λ) should blend two conceptually distinct components, which are most likely:

options.A: historical portfolio volatility and prospective portfolio volatility.
options.B: willingness to take risk and ability to take risk.
options.C: asset-side volatility and liability-side volatility.

rationales.A: Historical and prospective portfolio volatility are both quantitative estimates of the portfolio's risk, not components of the investor. Blending them says nothing about how the investor feels about loss or about the financial capacity to absorb it, which is what the risk aversion coefficient is meant to capture.
rationales.B: Best practice is to examine both the investor's preference for risk — willingness to take risk, a subjective measure focused on how the investor feels about and reacts to portfolio ups and downs — and the investor's capacity for taking risk, an objective measure of the ability to tolerate portfolio losses and the potential decrease in future consumption that follows. Risk preference and risk capacity are sometimes referred to as willingness and ability to take risk, respectively, and the coefficient used in the objective function should reflect a blend of the two.
rationales.C: Asset-side and liability-side volatility belong to liability-relative asset allocation, where the quantity of interest is the volatility of the surplus. That is a different framework from the assessment of an individual investor's risk aversion coefficient.

questions.stem: For an individual investor, risk capacity is most likely affected by:

options.A: the investor's score on a risk-tolerance questionnaire.
options.B: the investor's stated comfort with large portfolio drawdowns.
options.C: the investor's net worth, income, and savings rate.

rationales.A: A score on a validated psychometric questionnaire locates the investor's risk preference — the willingness to take risk. Risk capacity is a separate, objective matter of financial circumstances such as net worth, income, emergency reserves, and the rate of saving, none of which a questionnaire score measures.
rationales.B: Stated comfort with large drawdowns is a subjective report of willingness to take risk. It says nothing about the financial ability to absorb those losses without impairing future consumption, which is what capacity measures.
rationales.C: For individuals, risk capacity is affected by factors such as net worth, income, the size of an emergency fund in relation to consumption needs, and the rate at which the individual saves out of gross income. These are objective features of the investor's financial circumstances, which is precisely what distinguishes capacity from the preference that validated risk-tolerance questionnaires are designed to locate.

questions.stem: An investor must withdraw €60,000 in 12 months without invading principal. This shortfall concern is most likely incorporated into the asset allocation by:

options.A: allocating the entire portfolio to cash.
options.B: ranking allocations by Roy's safety-first ratio.
options.C: abandoning the utility-based framework.

rationales.A: Holding only cash does guarantee the €60,000 is available, but it abandons the return objective entirely and, over any longer horizon, introduces its own shortfall risk relative to spending needs. The trade-off between shortfall risk and return is meant to be managed inside the allocation decision, not escaped by giving up the return objective.
rationales.B: Two efficient allocations can tie on expected utility — for example, both producing a certainty-equivalent utility of 6.0% — in which case the utility criterion cannot choose between them. Roy's safety-first ratio, [E(R_P) − R_L]/σ_P, evaluated at the shortfall threshold R_L = 5%, then separates them: a ratio of 0.25 for the first allocation against 0.20 for the second, so the first is preferred because it minimizes the probability of falling below the threshold. The same concern can instead be imposed directly as a shortfall constraint within the optimization, which lets a specific goal-based requirement override a pure utility tie.
rationales.C: The utility framework accommodates shortfall concerns rather than conflicting with them. The safety-first ratio is applied to allocations that the utility function ranks as equivalent, and a shortfall constraint can be added to the optimization itself, so a withdrawal requirement gives no reason to discard utility maximization.

questions.stem: A constraint added to a mean-variance optimization to reflect client circumstances is least likely to:

options.A: set a range for an asset class allocation.
options.B: set a fixed allocation to a specific asset.
options.C: require the covariance matrix to be diagonal.

rationales.A: An allocation range — for instance, emerging market equity constrained to between 5% and 20% — is one of the five general types of constraint routinely added to a mean-variance optimization to reflect a client's circumstances.
rationales.B: A set allocation to a specific asset — for instance, 30% to real estate, or a fixed holding in a non-tradable asset the client already owns — is likewise one of the five general constraint types.
rationales.C: Requiring the covariance matrix to be diagonal is an assumption about the optimizer's inputs, not a client-circumstance constraint, and forcing every covariance to zero would misstate the risk the optimization is solving against. The five general constraint types are: (1) a set allocation to a specific asset, such as a non-tradable asset; (2) an allocation range; (3) an upper limit on alternatives arising from liquidity considerations; (4) a relative allocation of two assets, such as emerging market equity held below developed market equity; and (5) in a liability-relative setting, holding short the assets that represent the systematic characteristics of the liability.

questions.stem: The extension of the mean-variance objective function that accommodates investors who weight downside outcomes more heavily than equivalent gains, as in prospect theory, is most likely:

options.A: optimization with a risk-aversion coefficient of zero.
options.B: reverse optimization using market-cap weights.
options.C: mean-conditional value-at-risk optimization.

rationales.A: Setting the risk-aversion coefficient to zero removes risk from the objective function altogether, leaving pure expected-return maximization. That ignores risk rather than treating gains and losses asymmetrically, so it cannot capture the prospect-theory investor's preferences.
rationales.B: Reverse optimization infers expected returns from market-capitalization weights. It changes how the inputs are estimated, not the shape of the objective function, so the symmetric variance penalty remains in place and downside asymmetry is left unaddressed.
rationales.C: Prospect theory holds that the pain of a loss is approximately twice as significant as the joy of an equivalent gain, so the objective function must penalize downside outcomes more heavily than upside ones. The extensions that do this are mean-semivariance optimization (Markowitz 1959), mean-conditional value-at-risk optimization (Rockafellar and Uryasev 2000; Goldberg et al. 2013; Xiong and Idzorek 2011), mean-variance-skewness optimization (Briec et al. 2007; Harvey et al. 2010), and mean-variance-skewness-kurtosis optimization (Athayde and Flôres 2003; Beardsley et al. 2012).

drills.los_text: describe the use of investment factors in constructing and analyzing an asset allocation

questions.stem: In factor-based asset allocation, the factors used alongside the market factor least likely include:

options.A: size, valuation, and momentum.
options.B: duration, credit, liquidity, and volatility.
options.C: demographic trends and GDP growth.

rationales.A: Size, valuation (value versus growth), and momentum are among the typical factors used alongside the market factor. Most were originally identified as return drivers that help explain the portion of returns the CAPM leaves unexplained.
rationales.B: Duration or term, credit, liquidity, and volatility are also among the typical factors used alongside the all-important market (equity) exposure.
rationales.C: Demographic trends and GDP growth are macroeconomic drivers rather than portfolio factors. The typical factors are size, valuation, momentum, liquidity, duration (term), credit, and volatility, used alongside the market (equity) exposure; each is constructed from traded securities, whereas demographics and GDP growth are not directly investable exposures.

questions.stem: Apart from the market factor, factors in factor-based asset allocation are typically zero-investment, or self-financing. The size factor return is most likely:

options.A: the small-cap return less the large-cap return.
options.B: the weighted average of small-cap and large-cap returns.
options.C: the large-cap return plus the small-cap return.

rationales.A: Factors other than the market factor typically represent zero-investment, self-financing positions in which the underperforming attribute is sold short to finance an offsetting long position in the better-performing attribute. For the size factor this gives a factor return equal to the small-cap stock return minus the large-cap stock return, so if large-caps outperform small-caps the size factor return is negative.
rationales.B: A weighted average of small-cap and large-cap returns is the return on a long-only portfolio. It requires net capital rather than being self-financing, and because it holds both attributes long it does not isolate the size attribute at all.
rationales.C: Adding the two returns together is neither self-financing nor a return on any portfolio: it implies two units of long exposure funded with capital, and it rises whenever either capitalization segment rises, so it carries no information about the size attribute.

questions.stem: Constructing risk factors as zero-investment long-short positions most likely gives those factors correlations that are:

options.A: identical across all major asset classes.
options.B: low with the market and with one another.
options.C: perfectly positive with the market.

rationales.A: Zero-investment construction does nothing that would equalize a factor's correlations from one asset class to the next. Measured factor correlations differ across equities, fixed income, commodities and currencies, so correlations vary across asset classes rather than being identical.
rationales.B: Constructing factors as zero-investment positions removes most market exposure from the factors, because the short positions offset the long positions. What is left is the factor premium itself rather than broad market beta, so the factors generally have low correlations with the market and also low correlations with one another. That low cross-correlation is what makes a factor-based opportunity set attractive for diversification.
rationales.C: Perfect correlation with the market would require the factor to retain full market exposure. Zero-investment construction removes that exposure rather than preserving it: the short leg offsets the long leg, leaving a near market-neutral position whose correlation with the market is low, not one.

questions.stem: In practice, when factor-based asset allocation is done in 'total return space' alongside traditional asset classes, the factor return most likely needs to be augmented by:

options.A: The return on the risk-free asset held as collateral.
options.B: A random walk term calibrated to the factor's tracking error.
options.C: The return on the market portfolio.

rationales.A: To stay in total return space, the factor return needs to include the return on the assumed collateral, typically three-month Treasury bills. This adjustment is also needed if one plans to include both risk factors and some traditional asset classes in the same optimization, because the asset classes are quoted as total returns. One way to think about a self-financing allocation to a risk factor is that in order to invest in it, an investor must put up an equivalent amount of collateral invested in cash, so the factor's total return is the risk-free rate plus the excess factor return.
rationales.B: No random term is added. Moving a long-short factor into total return space is a deterministic adjustment: the risk-free rate on the collateral converts the excess factor return into a total return comparable with asset class returns. Tracking error describes the factor's dispersion, not the level of return that has to be added back.
rationales.C: The market is itself a separate factor in this framework. Adding the market return to every factor would give each factor the equity premium a second time and double-count equity beta, leaving the optimization with inputs that are not comparable with the traditional asset classes alongside them.

questions.stem: A practitioner choosing between factor-based and asset-class-based asset allocation is most likely advised to:

options.A: favour factor space whenever derivatives are permitted, as factors diversify better.
options.B: choose the space in which he or she is best equipped to make capital market assumptions.
options.C: work in asset class space, as factor assumptions cannot be made reliably.

rationales.A: There is no derivatives-based preference rule, and factors are not inherently more diversified than asset classes for a given level of forecasting skill. The recommendation is space-neutral: it hinges on where the practitioner's capital market assumptions are best made, not on the instruments available for implementation.
rationales.B: Practitioners should choose to carry out asset allocation in the particular space, risk factors or asset classes, in which they are most equipped to make capital market assumptions. Regardless of which space a practitioner prefers, expanding the opportunity set to include new, weakly correlated risk factors or asset classes should improve the potential risk-return trade-offs.
rationales.C: Factor assumptions are not deemed inherently unreliable, so there is no general instruction to retreat to asset class space. The guidance is to work in whichever space, risk factors or asset classes, the practitioner is best equipped to make capital market assumptions in.

drills.los_text: describe and evaluate characteristics of liabilities that are relevant to asset allocation

questions.stem: An example of a contingent liability is most likely:

options.A: A fixed-rate mortgage with level monthly payments.
options.B: The liabilities of a defined benefit pension plan.
options.C: A fixed-coupon corporate bond issued at par.

rationales.A: A mortgage with a fixed interest rate and fixed monthly payments has both its amounts and its dates known in advance, which makes it a fixed liability. Nothing about the obligation waits on an uncertain future event.
rationales.B: Defined benefit pension plans are an important example of contingent liabilities. The plan sponsor has a legal commitment to pay beneficiaries, but the exact dates and amounts of those payments depend on employees' retirement dates, their longevity, and the plan's cash payout rules. Insurance company liabilities are contingent in the same way: payment depends on the occurrence of a predefined event.
rationales.C: A fixed-coupon bond issued at par has a known coupon, a known principal and a known payment schedule, so both the amounts and the timing are set at issuance. That is the definition of a fixed liability, not a contingent one.

questions.stem: An example of a quasi-liability is most likely:

options.A: A corporate bond obligation of a university's financing arm.
options.B: An insurance policy payout owed to a policyholder.
options.C: The operating budget support a university expects from its endowment.

rationales.A: A bond's coupon and principal schedule is a legal liability, enforceable in court by the bondholders. A quasi-liability, by contrast, is a payment the institution expects to make and treats as essential, with no legal enforceability behind it.
rationales.B: Policy payouts are contractual obligations of the insurer and therefore legal liabilities, even though their timing is contingent on an insured event. The quasi-liability is the payment that is expected but not legally required, such as endowment support of a university's operating budget.
rationales.C: Legal liabilities are distinguished from cash payments that are expected to be made in the future and are essential to the mission of an institution but are not legal liabilities. The endowment of a university fits this second category: the endowment contributes a major part of the university's operating budget and assures stakeholders that it will continue such support, yet there is no legal enforceability. An individual's spending needs are quasi-liabilities in the same sense.

questions.stem: A characteristic of an institution's liabilities that is relevant to its asset allocation is least likely:

options.A: the historical dividend yield of the sponsor's equity.
options.B: the duration and convexity of liability cash flows.
options.C: the factors driving future liability cash flows.

rationales.A: The dividend yield on the sponsoring organization's own shares is not a liability characteristic at all; it describes the sponsor's equity, not the obligations being funded. The seven liability characteristics relevant to asset allocation are: fixed versus contingent cash flows; legal versus quasi-liabilities; duration and convexity of liability cash flows; the value of the liabilities relative to the size of the sponsoring organization; the factors driving future liability cash flows, namely inflation, economic conditions, interest rates and risk premiums; timing considerations such as longevity risk; and regulations affecting the calculation of liability cash flows.
rationales.B: Duration and convexity of the liability cash flows are among the seven characteristics. They determine how the present value of the liabilities responds to interest rate changes, which is what a hedging portfolio has to match.
rationales.C: The factors driving future liability cash flows, including inflation, economic conditions, interest rates and risk premiums, are among the seven characteristics. They tell the investor which asset exposures will move with the liabilities.

questions.stem: Lowtech Company's frozen defined benefit pension plan holds assets of US$2.5 billion. The present value of its projected liabilities is US$2.261 billion at a 4% discount rate and US$3.039 billion at a 2% discount rate. The plan's funding ratio at the 4% discount rate is closest to:

rationales.A: This overstates the funding ratio. Dividing the US$2.5 billion market value of assets by the US$2.261 billion present value of liabilities gives 1.1057, not 1.32; a ratio of 1.32 would require liabilities of roughly US$1.9 billion, which is below the present value at either discount rate given.
rationales.B: Funding ratio = Market value of assets / Present value of liabilities = US$2.5 billion / US$2.261 billion = 1.1057, so the plan is about 10.6% overfunded at the 4% discount rate. The surplus is US$2.5 billion minus US$2.261 billion, or US$0.239 billion. Note how sensitive this is to the discount rate: at 2% the same liabilities are worth US$3.039 billion, the funding ratio falls to 0.8226, and the surplus turns negative at minus US$0.539 billion.
rationales.C: This is the funding ratio at the 2% discount rate: US$2.5 billion / US$3.039 billion = 0.8226, leaving the plan underfunded by US$0.539 billion. The question asks for the ratio at the 4% discount rate, where the lower liability present value of US$2.261 billion produces a ratio above 1.

questions.stem: The discount rate applied to an institution's liabilities is most likely determined by:

options.A: Regulations, tradition, and the return on assets that would hedge the liabilities.
options.B: The sponsor's weighted-average cost of debt.
options.C: The expected return on the fund's asset portfolio.

rationales.A: The choice of discount rate is generally set by regulations and tradition. From the standpoint of economic theory, if the liability cash flows can be hedged perfectly by a set of market-priced assets, the discount rate can be determined by reference to the discount rate for those assets. For example, if pension liabilities are fixed, the discount rate should be the risk-free rate with reference to the duration of the liability cash flows.
rationales.B: The sponsor's cost of debt is a financing cost for the organization, not the theoretically correct rate for valuing the obligations. Regulations, tradition, and the rate on the assets that would perfectly hedge the liability cash flows govern the choice instead.
rationales.C: Discounting at the expected return on assets makes the reported value of the liabilities depend on the asset mix chosen to fund them, so a riskier portfolio would appear to shrink the liability. That is circular and theoretically unsound: the liability's value should reflect the cash flows and the assets that would hedge them, not the sponsor's investment policy.

drills.los_text: discuss approaches to liability-relative asset allocation

questions.stem: An approach to liability-relative asset allocation is least likely:

options.A: hedging/return-seeking portfolios.
options.B: surplus optimization.
options.C: equal-weight liability apportionment.

rationales.A: The hedging/return-seeking split, also called the two-portfolio approach, is one of the three approaches. Assets are divided into a hedging portfolio that covers the liabilities and a return-seeking portfolio that is invested for growth, which requires a surplus to fund.
rationales.B: Surplus optimization is one of the three approaches. It extends mean-variance optimization by using the volatility of surplus, the market value of assets minus the present value of liabilities, as the risk measure in place of asset volatility.
rationales.C: Equal-weight apportionment across liability tranches is not one of the three approaches. The three are surplus optimization; the hedging/return-seeking two-portfolio approach; and the integrated asset-liability approach, which is used by banks, insurance companies, and long-short hedge funds that make joint decisions about assets and liabilities.

questions.stem: Surplus optimization is most likely best described as:

options.A: An extension of mean-variance optimization applied to surplus returns.
options.B: A cash flow matching technique that involves no optimization.
options.C: A framework distinct from mean-variance optimization, with no objective function.

rationales.A: Surplus optimization adapts asset-only mean-variance optimization by substituting surplus return for asset return over a given time horizon. The objective function becomes U_LR = E(R_s,m) minus 0.005 times lambda times the variance of R_s,m, where the surplus return R_s equals (Change in asset value minus Change in liability value) divided by the initial asset value. It is a straightforward extension of the asset-only portfolio model rather than a new framework.
rationales.B: Cash flow matching pairs each liability payment with a dedicated bond, which is a way of constructing a hedging portfolio, not surplus optimization. Surplus optimization runs an optimization: it maximizes a mean-variance objective function defined over the surplus return, trading expected surplus return against surplus volatility at the investor's risk aversion.
rationales.C: Surplus optimization is an extension of mean-variance optimization, not a departure from it. The same mean-variance machinery and the same quadratic objective function are retained; only the input changes, from asset return and asset volatility to surplus return and surplus volatility.

questions.stem: Which of the following is least likely a step in the surplus optimization approach?

options.A: Estimating expected returns and volatilities for assets and liabilities.
options.B: Adjusting the discount rate to make the funding ratio equal one.
options.C: Selecting asset categories and the planning horizon.

rationales.A: This is step 2: estimating expected returns and volatilities for the asset categories and estimating liability returns, which is what produces the expanded matrix that carries the liabilities alongside the assets.
rationales.B: Adjusting the discount rate to force the funding ratio to equal one is not one of the six steps; moving the discount rate changes the measured present value of the liabilities rather than allocating any assets. The six steps are: (1) select asset categories and determine the planning horizon, (2) estimate expected returns and volatilities for the asset categories and estimate liability returns, giving the expanded matrix, (3) determine the constraints on the investment mix, (4) estimate the expanded correlation matrix and the volatilities, (5) compute the surplus efficient frontier and compare it with the asset-only efficient frontier, and (6) select the recommended portfolio mix.
rationales.C: This is step 1: selecting the asset categories and determining the planning horizon, which frames the optimization before any return or volatility estimate is made.

questions.stem: In its basic case, the hedging/return-seeking (two-portfolio) approach is most appropriate for:

options.A: underfunded plans that must take on risk to close a deficit.
options.B: investors with no market for hedging instruments.
options.C: conservative investors and overfunded pension plans.

rationales.A: Underfunded plans require variants of the two-portfolio approach rather than the basic version: with no surplus there is nothing to place in the return-seeking portfolio, so the sponsor raises contributions or turns to a partial hedge or a dynamic glide path.
rationales.B: The basic approach relies on well-functioning hedging markets rather than on their absence, and it applies in many contexts, not only where hedging instruments are unavailable.
rationales.C: The basic two-portfolio approach is most appropriate for conservative investors, such as insurance companies, and for overfunded pension plans that wish to reduce or eliminate the risk of not being able to pay future liabilities. In a basic application with US$2.5B of assets and liabilities of US$2.261B at a 4% discount rate, US$2.261B is invested in the hedging portfolio (long bonds matched to the 4% discount rate) and the remaining US$0.239B of surplus goes to the return-seeking portfolio.

questions.stem: The integrated asset-liability approach is most appropriate for institutional investors that:

options.A: make asset allocation decisions independently of liability decisions.
options.B: can fully defease their liabilities with a dedicated bond portfolio.
options.C: decide the composition of their liabilities jointly with asset allocation.

rationales.A: Deciding asset allocation independently of the liabilities describes the setting for surplus optimization or for the two-portfolio approach, not for the integrated approach, whose whole point is that the two sets of decisions are taken together.
rationales.B: Fully defeasible liabilities call for a hedging or cash-flow-matching portfolio, not for integrated modeling; the integrated approach fits institutions whose liability composition is itself a decision made jointly with asset allocation.
rationales.C: Integrated asset-liability approaches are appropriate for institutions where asset and liability decisions can be integrated and jointly optimized: banks, long-short hedge funds (where the short positions are liabilities), insurance companies and reinsurance companies. Such institutions must render significant decisions about the composition of their liabilities. The approach is known as ALM in banking and as dynamic financial analysis (DFA) in insurance, and it is often implemented in multi-period models.

drills.los_text: recommend and justify a liability-relative asset allocation

questions.stem: For an overfunded pension plan with fixed (frozen) liabilities that wishes to reduce risk of underfunding, the most appropriate liability-relative approach is most likely:

options.A: the basic hedging/return-seeking two-portfolio approach.
options.B: an aggressive equity-only allocation.
options.C: the integrated asset-liability approach.

rationales.A: The basic two-portfolio approach is the one identified as most appropriate for conservative investors and for overfunded pension plans wishing to eliminate the risk of not being able to pay liabilities: invest the present value of the liabilities in a hedging portfolio and the surplus in a return-seeking portfolio. With US$2.5B of assets against US$2.261B of liabilities discounted at 4%, US$2.261B goes to the hedging portfolio of long bonds and the US$0.239B surplus to the return-seeking portfolio.
rationales.B: An aggressive equity-only allocation ignores the liability structure altogether, chasing surplus growth at the cost of the very underfunding risk the plan wants to reduce.
rationales.C: The integrated asset-liability approach, with dynamic multi-period optimization, applies where the composition of the liabilities is itself a decision, as at banks and insurers. A frozen defined benefit plan's liabilities are fixed, so there is nothing on the liability side left to optimize.

questions.stem: For an underfunded pension plan, the basic two-portfolio approach most likely does not apply because:

options.A: surplus optimization always outperforms it in this case.
options.B: it requires perfect liquidity in all liability-hedging instruments.
options.C: there is no surplus to allocate to the return-seeking portfolio.

rationales.A: No claim is made that surplus optimization always outperforms the two-portfolio approach for an underfunded plan; what disqualifies the basic approach is the absence of a surplus, not relative performance.
rationales.B: The basic approach does not require perfect liquidity in every liability-hedging instrument. The obstacle for an underfunded plan is structural: there is no surplus to invest in the return-seeking portfolio.
rationales.C: When the plan is underfunded — for example a surplus of −US$0.539B once the liabilities are discounted at 2% — nothing is left over for the return-seeking portfolio. The sponsor would either develop a strategy to raise the funding ratio, through higher contributions, or apply a variant of the two-portfolio approach. Variants include a partial hedge, which reduces the allocation to the hedging portfolio in order to seek higher returns, and dynamic versions that follow a glide path, increasing the hedging portfolio as the funding ratio improves.

questions.stem: Comparing two efficient mixes on a surplus efficient frontier, one at a low expected surplus return and one at a higher expected surplus return, the allocation to corporate bonds, which hedge the liabilities, is most likely:

options.A: identical in the two mixes.
options.B: substantially larger in the lower-surplus-return mix.
options.C: substantially larger in the higher-surplus-return mix.

rationales.A: The two mixes are substantively different, and the difference sits precisely in the allocation to the hedging asset.
rationales.B: The low-surplus-return portfolio holds a substantial position in corporate bonds, while the high-surplus-return mix does not include them at all. The allocation to corporate bonds declines as expected surplus return increases because the price of the bonds is positively correlated with the present value of the liabilities: that correlation is what makes corporate bonds the hedging asset, and the hedging asset is employed most heavily at the low end of the surplus efficient frontier. Moving from an efficient mix with US$0.26 billion of expected surplus return to one with US$0.32 billion reduces or eliminates the corporate bond holding.
rationales.C: This reverses the relationship. The corporate bond allocation falls, rather than rises, as expected surplus return increases, because the bonds are held to hedge the present value of the liabilities and not to generate surplus.

questions.stem: For a property/casualty insurer with catastrophic-risk liabilities such as earthquakes and hurricanes, the most appropriate conclusion is most likely that:

options.A: catastrophe-exposed policies should not be written.
options.B: the hedging portfolio is ill-defined, so reinsurance is used.
options.C: the hedging portfolio is well-defined and easily built.

rationales.A: Bearing these risks is the property/casualty business itself, so withdrawal is not the response to an ill-defined hedging portfolio. The liabilities are instead addressed through customized products or by purchasing reinsurance.
rationales.B: For property/casualty insurance with catastrophic liabilities the hedging portfolio is not well-defined: a book of catastrophic-risk policies is difficult to hedge. Those liabilities might instead be addressed through customized products or by purchasing reinsurance. The assets and the liabilities are integrated, so that worst-case events can be analyzed on both sides of the balance sheet, and tail risk measures such as 1% VaR and conditional VaR determine how much capital is needed.
rationales.C: Earthquake and hurricane liabilities have no well-defined hedging portfolio in traditional markets, so a hedge cannot be assembled out of listed securities. That is exactly why customized products and reinsurance are used instead, and why the balance sheet is analyzed as an integrated whole.

questions.stem: A factor-based approach to liability-relative asset allocation is most likely credible because:

options.A: liability cash flows depend on multiple uncertain factors.
options.B: liability duration can be hedged only through factor exposures.
options.C: factor portfolios earn higher expected returns at the same risk.

rationales.A: A factor-based approach to liability-relative allocation has gained credibility because in many applications the liability cash flows are dependent on multiple uncertainties. The two primary macro factors are future economic conditions and inflation, with salary changes mattering as well for an ongoing scheme. When liabilities are driven by such uncertain factors, a fully hedged portfolio cannot be constructed; for an ongoing pension scheme the best that can be done is to add asset categories positively correlated with the underlying driving risk factors, such as inflation-linked bonds.
rationales.B: Liability duration can be hedged with a conventional bond portfolio, so factor exposures are not the only route. The factor approach earns its credibility from the fact that a fully hedged portfolio cannot be constructed when liability cash flows depend on uncertain macro factors, which is why asset categories positively correlated with those factors, such as inflation-linked bonds, are added instead.
rationales.C: No claim of superior risk-adjusted returns is made for factor portfolios. The credibility of the factor approach rests on liability cash flows being driven by multiple uncertain factors — economic conditions, inflation and salary changes — and on the impossibility of a fully hedged portfolio under those conditions, not on a return advantage at a given level of risk.

drills.los_text: recommend and justify an asset allocation using a goals-based approach

questions.stem: The goals-based asset allocation process most likely disaggregates the investor's portfolio into:

options.A: a single portfolio optimized against one utility function.
options.B: an equal-weighted portfolio of all available asset classes.
options.C: sub-portfolios, each funding one goal with its own horizon.

rationales.A: One portfolio optimized against a single comprehensive utility function is the traditional approach, which is precisely what goals-based allocation departs from: no part of such a portfolio is tied to any particular goal.
rationales.B: An equal weight in every available asset class is the 1/N heuristic. It is a naive diversification rule, not a goals-based process, and it attaches no sub-portfolio to a goal, a horizon or a required probability of success.
rationales.C: A goals-based asset allocation process disaggregates the investor's portfolio into a number of sub-portfolios, each of which is designed to fund an individual goal, or mental account, with its own time horizon and its own required probability of success. This addresses the Shefrin-Statman behavioral portfolio concept, and it rests on the Das, Markowitz, Scheid and Statman (2010, 2011) demonstration that traditional and behavioral finance are equivalent once risk is redefined from volatility to the probability of not achieving a goal.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about how institutions and individuals define investment goals is most likely correct?

options.A: Individuals have single goals and institutions multiple.
options.B: Both groups define risk as return volatility.
options.C: Individuals have multiple goals and institutions single.

rationales.A: This reverses the comparison. It is individuals who carry multiple goals, each with its own horizon, while an institution typically works to one goal over one horizon.
rationales.B: The risk measures differ rather than coincide: institutions typically measure risk as volatility, of return or of surplus, while individuals measure it as the probability of missing a goal.
rationales.C: Institutions typically have a single goal with a single time horizon, whereas individuals have multiple goals with multiple time horizons. Institutions generally use volatility, of return or of surplus, as the risk measure and mathematical expectations to determine return requirements; individuals use the probability of missing a goal and minimum expectations. Institutions are also often tax-exempt, while individuals are mostly taxable.

questions.stem: Minimum expectations in goals-based asset allocation are most likely defined as:

options.A: The lowest return observed historically for the asset mix.
options.B: The minimum return expected over the horizon at a given required probability of success.
options.C: The arithmetic mean of expected returns over the goal's horizon.

rationales.A: Historical minima are backward-looking, and a single worst observed outcome is not a probability statement. Minimum expectations are a forward-looking return floor set at a stated confidence level, so the lowest return ever recorded for the recommended asset mix does not define them.
rationales.B: Minimum expectations are defined as the minimum return expected to be earned over a given time horizon with a given minimum required probability of success. For example, a portfolio with a 7% expected return and 10% volatility, held over five years with a 90% required probability of success, produces only about 1.3% per year of compound return at that 90% probability level. That is a considerably lower discount rate than the 7% average, so a larger capital reservation is required to defease the goal.
rationales.C: The plain expected return, whether arithmetic or compound, carries no success-probability qualifier. Minimum expectations attach a required probability to the horizon return, which pulls the usable discount rate well below the mean and raises the capital required to fund the goal.

questions.curriculum_ref: Developing Goals-Based Asset Allocations — minimum expectations

questions.stem: Under the goals-based approach, a portfolio with expected annual return 7%, volatility 10%, target 5-year horizon, and 90% required probability of success most likely implies a defeasance discount rate closest to:

options.A: 7.0% per year.
options.B: 0.0% per year.
options.C: 1.3% per year.

rationales.A: Discounting at the 7% expected return ignores the required probability of success. It is the rate along the central or expected path, not the rate the portfolio is expected to exceed with 90% probability, so it would understate the capital needed to defease the goal.
rationales.B: A 90% required probability of success does not demand certainty, so the probability-adjusted rate is reduced below the 7% mean but remains positive. Here it is approximately 1.3% per year, not zero; a zero rate would correspond to requiring that the goal be met with certainty.
rationales.C: Over five years the portfolio is expected to produce total returns of 35% (= 5 × 7%), with five-year volatility of 22.4% (= 10% × √5) under an IID assumption. The 90% probability return level sits roughly 1.28 standard deviations below the mean, far below the median outcome, which implies a compound return of about 1.3% per year at that 90% probability level. This lower rate is the one used to determine the capital required for the goal.

questions.curriculum_ref: Developing Goals-Based Asset Allocations — worked example

questions.stem: Under a goals-based asset allocation approach, risk is most likely measured as:

options.A: The tracking error against a policy benchmark.
options.B: The probability of not achieving each specific goal.
options.C: The volatility of overall portfolio returns.

rationales.A: Tracking error against a policy benchmark is a professional-portfolio-management measure of relative risk. It says nothing about whether an individual's goal will be funded, which is what the goals-based framework measures.
rationales.B: Das, Markowitz, Scheid, and Statman (2010, 2011) show that traditional and behavioral finance are equivalent if the definition of risk is changed from the volatility of returns to the probability of not achieving a goal. For individuals, the risk measure is therefore the probability of missing the goal, and each goal may be assigned its own required probability of success — a high probability for an essential need, a lower one for an aspirational wish.
rationales.C: The volatility of overall portfolio returns is the traditional mean-variance risk measure. It aggregates risk at the portfolio level and treats all shortfalls alike, rather than asking goal by goal how likely each one is to be missed.

drills.los_text: describe and evaluate heuristic and other approaches to asset allocation

questions.stem: The '120 minus your age' heuristic (or the older '100 minus your age') most likely implies:

options.A: A linear decrease in equity allocation as the investor ages.
options.B: An increase in equity allocation as the investor ages.
options.C: A constant equity allocation regardless of age.

rationales.A: The heuristic sets 120 − Age = percentage allocated to stocks. Although no theoretic basis is identified for it, the result is a linear decrease in equity exposure that seems to fit the general equity glide paths of target-date funds, including those built on a total balance sheet approach that incorporates human capital. A 25-year-old would allocate 95% to stocks and a 76-year-old 44%.
rationales.B: This reverses the relationship. Because age is subtracted, 120 − Age falls as the investor gets older, so equity exposure declines rather than rises.
rationales.C: The allocation is age-linked, not fixed: subtracting age from 120 gives 95% equity at age 25 and 44% at age 76, a steady decline rather than a constant weight.

questions.stem: The 60/40 stock/bond heuristic is most likely:

options.A: Supported by partial empirical evidence.
options.B: Optimal for every investor.
options.C: Arbitrary, with no empirical support.

rationales.A: There is some evidence that the global financial asset market portfolio is close to this prototypical 60/40 split. Doeswijk, Lam, and Swinkels (2014) show that in approximately 7 of the 23 years from 1990 to 2012, equities, private equity, and real estate accounted for slightly more than 60% of the global market portfolio, and for the remaining years the combined share was slightly less. That is partial, heuristic support for the split rather than a derivation of it.
rationales.B: The 60/40 mix is treated as a heuristic, not as a universally optimal allocation. It takes no account of an investor's objectives, time horizon, liabilities, or risk tolerance, any of which can justify a very different mix.
rationales.C: The split is not without empirical grounding: the global market portfolio has hovered near a 60/40 division between risky and fixed-income assets, which is why the heuristic has partial support even though it is not optimized for any individual investor.

questions.stem: The Yale endowment model (or 'Yale model') as described by Swensen is most likely characterized by:

options.A: Large allocations to illiquid, actively managed non-traditional assets.
options.B: Passive, market-cap-weighted holdings of publicly traded securities.
options.C: Equal risk contributions from every asset.

rationales.A: The endowment model, pioneered by Swensen at Yale, is characterized by large allocations to non-traditional investments, including equity-oriented investments driven by manager skill such as private equity, a strong commitment to active management, and the pursuit of illiquidity premiums that an endowment with a long time horizon is well positioned to capture. Yale's 2014 allocation showed 33.0% private equity, 17.6% real estate, and 17.4% absolute return, far above the means for US educational institutions.
rationales.B: Passive, market-cap-weighted exposure to publicly traded securities describes the Norway model, which reflects a belief in market informational efficiency. It is close to the diametrical opposite of the endowment model's reliance on active management and illiquid assets.
rationales.C: Equalizing each asset's contribution to total portfolio risk is risk parity, a separate approach that addresses the concentration of risk sources in mean-variance allocations. It is not a feature of the endowment model.

questions.stem: A risk parity asset allocation is most likely based on the notion that:

options.A: the highest-Sharpe-ratio asset should receive the largest weight.
options.B: each asset should be held at its global market-cap weight.
options.C: each asset should contribute equally to total portfolio risk.

rationales.A: Weighting by Sharpe ratio is not the risk parity criterion. Risk parity equalizes risk contributions and is indifferent to which asset offers the best risk-adjusted return, which is one reason it is criticized for ignoring expected returns altogether.
rationales.B: Holding each asset at its global market-cap weight is market-cap weighting, the basis of the global market portfolio, not risk parity. Market-cap weights typically leave risk heavily concentrated in equities, which is exactly the outcome risk parity is designed to avoid.
rationales.C: A risk parity allocation is based on the notion that each asset — asset class or risk factor — should contribute equally to the total risk of the portfolio for the portfolio to be well diversified. The condition is w_i × Cov(r_i, r_P) = (1/n) × σ²_P, so each asset's covariance-weighted contribution equals a 1/n share of portfolio variance. This responds to the criticism that mean-variance allocations can look diversified across assets while their sources of risk are not.

questions.stem: Empirical evidence on the 1/N rule (equal weighting across N assets) most likely shows that it:

options.A: performs better than theory would suggest.
options.B: matches optimized portfolios only when assets are identical.
options.C: underperforms every optimization-based method.

rationales.A: In principle, 1/N portfolios should be dominated by methods that optimize asset class weights to exploit differences in investment characteristics. Empirical studies, notably DeMiguel, Garlappi, and Uppal (2009), have instead found that 1/N performs considerably better than theory might suggest on measures such as Sharpe ratios and certainty equivalents. One explanation is that equal weighting sidesteps the problems caused by optimizing when there is estimation error in the inputs.
rationales.B: The empirical finding is not conditional on assets having identical expected returns and volatilities. 1/N has performed well in practice even though real assets differ substantially, and the likely reason is that it avoids optimizing over error-laden inputs rather than that the inputs happen to be equal.
rationales.C: The evidence points the other way. Rather than consistently losing to optimization-based methods, 1/N has held up well against them in out-of-sample tests, which is what makes the result notable.

questions.stem: Compared with the endowment model, the primary limitation of the Norway model (Norway Government Pension Fund Global) is most likely that it:

options.A: offers limited potential for above-market value added.
options.B: concentrates risk in the domestic economy.
options.C: requires aggressive leverage on bond holdings.

rationales.A: The Norway model is highly committed to passive investment in publicly traded securities, subject to ESG constraints, reflecting a belief in market informational efficiency, and has held an approximate 60/40 stock/bond mix since 2009. That brings low cost, transparency, suitability for very large scale, and straightforward governance, but it forgoes illiquidity premiums and active returns, leaving limited potential for above-market value added — almost diametrically opposite to the endowment model's pursuit of active management and illiquid assets.
rationales.B: The fund is deliberately invested globally; domestic concentration is precisely what it is designed to avoid, given that the sponsoring economy is already exposed to oil revenues. Concentration in Norwegian assets is therefore not a limitation of the model.
rationales.C: Leveraged bond exposure is a feature of risk parity implementations, which lever low-volatility assets to equalize risk contributions. The Norway model holds unlevered publicly traded stocks and bonds in an approximate 60/40 mix.

questions.stem: The two most common approaches to rebalancing an asset allocation are most likely:

options.A: Calendar rebalancing and percent-range rebalancing.
options.B: Immediate rebalancing and delayed rebalancing.
options.C: Buy-and-hold rebalancing and dollar-cost averaging.

rationales.A: Calendar rebalancing restores target weights at fixed periodic intervals — monthly, quarterly, semiannually, or annually — and keeps monitoring costs low. Percent-range rebalancing sets corridors around each target weight and is contingent on market movements, trading only when actual drift breaches a corridor, which makes it the more disciplined risk control policy.
rationales.B: Immediate and delayed rebalancing are not the standard categories. The timing distinction that matters is between acting on a fixed schedule and acting when weights drift outside a corridor; once a trigger is reached, how promptly a manager trades is an implementation detail, not a rebalancing framework.
rationales.C: Neither is a rebalancing approach. Buy-and-hold deliberately lets weights drift with the market and so is the absence of rebalancing, and dollar-cost averaging is a method of phasing new money into a portfolio rather than a rule for restoring target weights.

questions.stem: Rebalancing has empirically tended to reduce risk while incrementally adding to return. The two interpretations most often offered for that effect are most likely:

options.A: A momentum premium and a value premium.
options.B: A size premium and a quality premium.
options.C: A diversification return and a short volatility return.

rationales.A: Momentum and value are equity factor premia found in the cross-section of stocks; neither is one of the two interpretations offered for the rebalancing benefit. The rebalancing story is instead the diversification return and the return to supplying liquidity — buying the asset class that has weakened and selling the one that has strengthened.
rationales.B: Size and quality are cross-sectional stock factors, unrelated to the asset-class rebalancing benefit. Rebalancing trades across asset classes do not harvest them.
rationales.C: Two interpretations are offered. (1) Rebalancing earns a diversification return: the compound growth rate of a rebalanced portfolio is greater than the weighted-average compound growth rate of its components, so with sufficiently low transaction costs this produces a 'diversification return' from frequent rebalancing to a well-diversified portfolio (Willenbrock 2011). (2) Rebalancing earns a return from being short volatility: the return to a rebalanced portfolio can be replicated by a buy-and-hold position plus writing out-of-the-money puts and calls on the risky asset.

questions.stem: In percent-range rebalancing, all else equal, the factors that each widen an asset class's optimal corridor are most likely:

options.A: Lower transaction costs and higher volatility of the rest of the portfolio.
options.B: Higher liquidity of the asset class.
options.C: Higher transaction costs, higher risk tolerance, and higher correlation.

rationales.A: Lower transaction costs narrow corridors rather than widen them, because the benefit of rebalancing has a lower hurdle to clear. Higher volatility of the rest of the portfolio also narrows corridors, since large divergences from the strategic asset allocation become more likely.
rationales.B: Liquidity of the asset class is not one of the factors identified as driving optimal corridor width.
rationales.C: Factors positively related to optimal corridor width are transaction costs (higher costs mean the benefits of rebalancing must exceed a higher hurdle, so the corridor widens); risk tolerance (higher tolerance means less sensitivity to divergences from the strategic asset allocation, so the corridor widens); and correlation with the rest of the portfolio (higher correlation means further divergence is less likely, so the corridor widens). For taxable investors, higher capital gains tax rates also widen corridors.

questions.stem: In percent-range rebalancing, all else equal, the factor inversely related to an asset class's optimal corridor width is most likely:

options.A: Volatility of the rest of the portfolio.
options.B: Risk tolerance of the investor.
options.C: Transaction costs of the asset class.

rationales.A: The volatility of the rest of the portfolio is inversely related to the optimal corridor width. Higher volatility of the rest of the portfolio makes large divergences from the strategic asset allocation more likely, pointing to a narrower optimal corridor.
rationales.B: Risk tolerance is positively related to corridor width: a more risk-tolerant investor is less sensitive to divergences from the strategic asset allocation, so the corridor widens rather than narrows.
rationales.C: Transaction costs are positively related to corridor width: the higher the cost of trading, the higher the hurdle the benefits of rebalancing must exceed, so the corridor widens rather than narrows.

questions.stem: Holding all else equal is not really meaningful for an asset class's own volatility. Weighing that trade-off, the practical corridor width for an asset class is most likely:

options.A: Set equal to the volatility of the rest of the portfolio.
options.B: Set proportionally greater the higher its own volatility.
options.C: Set proportionally smaller the higher its own volatility.

rationales.A: Setting corridor width equal to the volatility of the rest of the portfolio is not the standard practice; practical corridors are scaled to the asset class's own volatility.
rationales.B: In practice, corridor width is often specified to be proportionally greater the higher an asset class's own volatility, with a focus on transaction cost control. In volatility-based rebalancing, corridor width is set proportionally to the asset class's own volatility. In equal probability rebalancing (McCalla 1997), the manager specifies a corridor for each asset class in terms of a common multiple of that class's standard deviation.
rationales.C: Specifying proportionally smaller corridors as own volatility rises ignores transaction costs: it would force the most frequent, and most expensive, trading in exactly the asset classes that move most.

questions.stem: In liability-relative asset allocation, rebalancing most likely includes:

options.A: Only adjusting asset weights back to strategic targets.
options.B: Adjusting the liability-hedging portfolio for net duration drift as well.
options.C: Resetting the liability discount rate to restore the funding ratio.

rationales.A: Rebalancing in a liability-relative framework is broader than returning the asset side to its strategic weights; it also covers the hedging portfolio's net duration exposure against the liability.
rationales.B: Rebalancing is the discipline of adjusting portfolio weights to align more closely with the strategic asset allocation. In liability-relative asset allocation, adjusting a liability-hedging portfolio to account for changes in net duration exposures from the passage of time falls under the rubric of rebalancing, so that the hedge maintains its intended relationship with the liability. That sits alongside correcting drift in the strategic asset weights.
rationales.C: The liability discount rate is set by regulation, tradition, or reference to hedging assets — it is not reset to engineer a funding ratio. Rebalancing adjusts portfolio weights and hedge exposures, not valuation assumptions.
